items.claim: This unit's woe-oracle onset at Jer.22.13 and its close at Jer.22.19 correctly bound one row, and it correctly treats the fourfold hoy of Jer.22.18 as a funeral-cry lament rather than a second woe onset.
items.evidence: Jer.22.13 opens with a bare hoy naming an unrighteous builder, “Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his rooms by injustice” (web:Jer.22.13), unveiled at Jer.22.18's therefore-clause as Jehoiakim; that same verse's four further hoy exclamations, “Ah my brother!” and “Ah sister!”, “Ah lord!” and “Ah his glory!” (web:Jer.22.18), are the denied funeral cries, a distinct role from the woe onset correctly kept apart in this unit's own signal tagging. The setumah marks at Jer.22.12, Jer.22.17, and this unit's own close at Jer.22.19 match the parashah inventory.

items.claim: This unit's discourse-imperative onset at Jer.22.20 carries a genuine seam from the Jehoiakim material just closed, its own rejected alternative already discloses the cedar/Lebanon continuity it might otherwise be charged with overlooking, and its silence on the ketiv/qere note at its own closing verse, Jer.22.23, is not a defect since only the WEB rendering of that verse is cited.
items.evidence: Jer.22.20 opens with the feminine-singular imperative “Go up to Lebanon, and cry out. Lift up your voice in Bashan” (web:Jer.22.20), addressed to a second-person figure rather than the third-person king just described; the rejected alternative names the shared cedar-house imagery and rejects reading this address as a continuation of the Jehoiakim woe on the addressee-shift ground, which is the strongest real rival available. Jer.22.23 carries two ketiv/qere notes per the inventory, but this unit only quotes the WEB English sense of that verse and makes no claim resting on its Hebrew ketiv or qere form, so the absence of a ketiv/qere disclosure is not a genuine defect. No parashah mark falls within Jer.22.20-Jer.22.23 itself, matching the inventory (only Jer.22.19, just before this unit's opening, carries a setumah).

items.claim: This unit's oath-formula onset at Jer.22.24 carries a genuine seam from the apostrophe just closed, and it correctly names the king by the Coniah throne-form at both of its own occurrences, distinct from the Jehoiachin and Jeconiah forms used at other sites in the book.
items.evidence: “As I live,” (web:Jer.22.24) says Yahweh, opens Jer.22.24 as a chai-ani oath formula distinct in shape from the imperative apostrophe of the material just closed; the king is named Coniah at both Jer.22.24 and Jer.22.28, the throne-form distinct from the Jehoiachin form (Jer.52.31) and the Jeconiah form used elsewhere in the book. Setumah marks at Jer.22.27 and Jer.22.29 match the parashah inventory; no mark falls on Jer.22.23, the verse just before this unit's opening.

items.claim: This unit correctly keeps the shepherds' woe together with the Davidic-Branch and new-exodus material as one divine speech, since none of the five neum-YHWH tags within its own span closes against a fresh addressee, scene, imperative, or date seam, and its type deviation from the woe-onset formula is disclosed rather than silently folded into the unit_type field.
items.evidence: The hoy woe-onset at Jer.23.1, “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” (web:Jer.23.1), is followed by five verses within this unit's own eight-verse span that carry a neum-YHWH tag (Jer.23.1, Jer.23.2, Jer.23.4, Jer.23.5, Jer.23.7), none of which is followed by a fresh addressee shift, scene shift, discourse imperative, date header, or vision opening before this unit's own close at Jer.23.8, so none of the five functions as a boundary driver. The type deviation -- a woe-formula onset governing a unit whose own bulk turns to a salvation promise once the shepherds are sentenced -- is disclosed in this unit's own device notes rather than folded into the unit_type field.

items.claim: This unit's rejected alternative asserts that Jer.23.13-Jer.23.14 continue "the same first-person indictment opened at" Jer.23.9, but Jer.23.9 carries the prophet's own unindicting first-person distress, not an indictment, and the indicting first-person voice is Yahweh's own, not established until Jer.23.11.
items.evidence: “My heart within me is broken. All my bones shake.” (web:Jer.23.9) is Jeremiah's own first-person reaction to the divine word: it levels no accusation against anyone and carries no neum-YHWH tag. The indicting first-person voice is Yahweh's own, established at Jer.23.11's “in my house I have found their wickedness” (web:Jer.23.11) (my house = the temple), closed by נְאֻם יְהוָֽה (byte tier), and again at Jer.23.12 by נְאֻם יְהוָֽה (byte tier), and continued through Jer.23.13's “I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria” (web:Jer.23.13) into the sentence at Jer.23.15. This unit's own account of its opening seam already distinguishes the prophet's first-person voice from the divine voice it displaces at Jer.23.9, so crediting Jer.23.9 with opening the same first-person indictment that Jer.23.13-Jer.23.14 continue is inconsistent with that same distinction.

items.claim: This unit's addressee-shift onset at Jer.23.16 and its closing rejection of extending into Jer.23.23's unaddressed self-predication both carry genuine seams, and its handling of the ketiv/qere verse at Jer.23.18 is correctly disclosed as consulted but not spliced.
items.evidence: Jer.23.16 opens with a second-person-plural imperative, “Don't listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you.” (web:Jer.23.16), a direct address distinct from the third-person sentence against the prophets just pronounced at Jer.23.15; the rejected alternative correctly identifies that Jer.23.23 drops this second-person address for an unaddressed divine self-predication, a genuine addressee-status shift even without a fresh imperative or koh-amar marker there. Jer.23.18, this unit's one ketiv/qere verse per the inventory, is only paraphrased for its general sense and never quoted in Hebrew, correctly avoiding any ketiv/qere conflation. The petuchah at Jer.23.15 preceding this unit's opening and the setumah marks at Jer.23.18 and Jer.23.22 match the parashah inventory.

items.claim: This unit correctly separates the neum-YHWH noun formula from the book's only finite-verb use of the same root within Jer.23.31, and correctly rejects a split at Jer.23.29-Jer.23.30 given the therefore-connective linking Jer.23.30 to the image just before it.
items.evidence: Jer.23.31 opens with the ordinary formula הִנְנִ֥י עַל הַנְּבִיאִ֖ם נְאֻם יְהוָ֑ה (noun neum followed by YHWH, byte tier) and continues with וַֽיִּנְאֲמ֖וּ נְאֻֽם (byte tier), where na'am functions as a finite verb governing its own cognate noun not followed by YHWH -- correctly kept apart from the formula count, and matching this its only verbal occurrence (sweep: 1 verse book-wide). Jer.23.30 opens with לָכֵ֛ן (therefore-equivalent, byte tier), a connective tying it to the fire-and-hammer image of Jer.23.29 rather than opening an independent unit, supporting the rejection of a split there; the threefold hineni-refrain (Jer.23.30, Jer.23.31, Jer.23.32) repeats the same hineni-al formula without an intervening addressee or speaker change.

items.claim: This unit correctly keeps the massa 'burden'/'oracle' wordplay as content disclosed in prose rather than folding it into the unit_type field, and its koh-amar clause at Jer.23.38 correctly carries the same divine speaker and the same offense across the whole span to the chapter's own close.
items.evidence: The unit_type is judgment_oracle, never a massa-based label (massa_oracle does not exist in this book's vocabulary), keeping the wordplay disclosed only in the boundary rationale and the literature-type description. Jer.23.38 opens לָכֵ֗ן כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה (therefore-Yahweh-says-equivalent, byte tier), continuing the same divine speaker and the same forbidden-phrase offense from Jer.23.33 with no addressee change through the close at Jer.23.40, immediately before Jer.24.1's fresh vision-report seeing-formula. The setumah at Jer.23.40, this unit's own close, matches the parashah inventory.
